html:
The sack of Rome was the plunder of the city of Rome by the Visigoths under their king Alaric, over three days from 24 August 410. It was the first time in about 800 years that the city had fallen to a foreign enemy.

Alaric's Goths had served Rome as allied troops but wanted land, pay and a Roman command. The western emperor Honorius, safe behind the marshes at Ravenna, which had replaced Rome as the capital, refused to deal. Alaric besieged Rome three times, and on the third someone opened a gate.

The Goths were Christians, and churches were largely spared. The damage was less than the shock. Rome was no longer the seat of government, but it was still the symbol of the empire, and news of its fall stunned the Roman world. Jerome wrote from Bethlehem that the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken. Augustine wrote The City of God partly to answer pagans who blamed the disaster on Christianity.

Alaric died months later in southern Italy. His people moved on to Gaul and Spain, and the sack became one of the landmarks of the Migration Period. The Vandals sacked Rome again in 455, and the western empire ended in 476.
